claim: Metabolic network rewiring is the rerouting of metabolism through the use of alternate enzymes to adjust pathway flux and accomplish specific anabolic or catabolic objectives.
source: Metabolic network rewiring is the rerouting of metabolism through the use of alternate enzymes to adjust pathway flux and accomplish specific anabolic or catabolic objectives.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that draws from established scientific understanding of metabolic network rewiring.

claim: C. elegans has two parallel pathways for the breakdown of the short chain fatty acid propionate.
source: Here, we report the first characterization of two parallel pathways for the breakdown of the short chain fatty acid propionate in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic interaction mapping, gene co-expression analysis, pathway intermediate quantification and carbon tracing experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: A vitamin B12-independent propionate breakdown shunt is transcriptionally activated on vitamin B12 deficient diets in C. elegans.
source: Using genetic interaction mapping, gene co-expression analysis, pathway intermediate quantification and carbon tracing, we uncover a vitamin B12-independent propionate breakdown shunt that is transcriptionally activated on vitamin B12 deficient diets, or under genetic conditions mimicking the human diseases propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia, in which the canonical B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway is blocked.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including gene expression analysis and genetic studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The propionate shunt is transcriptionally activated under genetic conditions mimicking propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia.
source: Using genetic interaction mapping, gene co-expression analysis, pathway intermediate quantification and carbon tracing, we uncover a vitamin B12-independent propionate breakdown shunt that is transcriptionally activated on vitamin B12 deficient diets, or under genetic conditions mimicking the human diseases propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia, in which the canonical B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway is blocked.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with pcca-1 mutants and other genetic perturbations described in the manuscript.

claim: This study presents the first example of transcriptional vitamin-directed metabolic network rewiring to promote survival under vitamin deficiency.
source: Our study presents the first example of transcriptional vitamin-directed metabolic network rewiring to promote survival under vitamin deficiency.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, supported by the experimental data presented and the lack of prior reports of such mechanisms.

claim: The ability to reroute propionate breakdown according to B12 availability may provide C. elegans with metabolic plasticity and a selective advantage on different diets in the wild.
source: The ability to reroute propionate breakdown according to B12 availability may provide C. elegans with metabolic plasticity and thus a selective advantage on different diets in the wild.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: Metabolic network rewiring can occur by transcriptional, post-transcriptional, or allosteric mechanisms.
source: Metabolic network rewiring to adjust metabolic flux in response to dietary or cellular cues can occur by transcriptional, post-transcriptional, or allosteric mechanisms (Desvergne et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genes encoding enzymes involved in the breakdown of galactose in the Leloir pathway are activated in yeast and other organisms upon a shift from glucose to galactose as a carbon source.
source: For instance, genes encoding enzymes involved in the breakdown of galactose in the Leloir pathway are activated in yeast and other organisms upon a shift from glucose to galactose as a carbon source (Fridovich-Keil, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In both yeast and humans, glycolytic flux is temporarily re-routed through the pentose phosphate pathway to provide a first-line protection against oxidative stress.
source: As a second example, in both yeast and humans, glycolytic flux is temporarily re-routed through the pentose phosphate pathway to provide a first-line protection against oxidative stress (Stincone et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Metabolic network rewiring to compensate for the absence of a vitamin or due to the toxic accumulation of a cellular metabolite has not yet been described prior to this study.
source: However, metabolic network rewiring to compensate for the absence of a vitamin or due to the toxic accumulation of a cellular metabolite has not yet been described.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on the absence of prior reports in the literature.

claim: In both mammals and C. elegans, vitamin B12 is a critical cofactor in the canonical propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway.
source: In both mammals and the nematode C. elegans, vitamin B12 is a critical cofactor in the canonical propionyl-CoA breakdown pathway (Figure 1A and 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of vitamin B12 in propionate metabolism, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Propionyl-CoA is produced during the catabolism of odd chain fatty acids and branched chain amino acids.
source: Propionyl-CoA is produced during the catabolism of odd chain fatty acids and branched chain amino acids, and is interconverted with the short chain fatty acid propionate derived from bacterial fermentation of dietary fibers in the intestine (Kasubuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Propionate is derived from bacterial fermentation of dietary fibers in the intestine.
source: Propionyl-CoA is produced during the catabolism of odd chain fatty acids and branched chain amino acids, and is interconverted with the short chain fatty acid propionate derived from bacterial fermentation of dietary fibers in the intestine (Kasubuchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae utilizes the methylcitrate cycle for propionate breakdown.
source: For instance, Saccharomyces cerevisiae utilizes the methylcitrate cycle, whereas plants and Candida albicans use a β-oxidation-like pathway (Halarnkar and Blomquist, 1989; Otzen et al., 2014) (diagrammed in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Plants and Candida albicans use a β-oxidation-like pathway for propionate breakdown.
source: For instance, Saccharomyces cerevisiae utilizes the methylcitrate cycle, whereas plants and Candida albicans use a β-oxidation-like pathway (Halarnkar and Blomquist, 1989; Otzen et al., 2014) (diagrammed in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutations in genes in the canonical vitamin B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway cause propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias.
source: Mutations in genes in the canonical vitamin B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway cause propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias, diseases in which propionate and its derivatives accumulate to toxic levels (La Marca et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias, propionate and its derivatives accumulate to toxic levels.
source: Mutations in genes in the canonical vitamin B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway cause propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias, diseases in which propionate and its derivatives accumulate to toxic levels (La Marca et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias are diagnosed by elevated levels of specific metabolites such as 3-hydroxypropionate (3-HP).
source: These diseases are diagnosed by elevated levels of specific metabolites such as 3-hydroxypropionate (3-HP), which is not normally detected at appreciable levels in healthy individuals (Matsumoto and Kuhara, 1996) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: 3-HP is not normally detected at appreciable levels in healthy individuals.
source: These diseases are diagnosed by elevated levels of specific metabolites such as 3-hydroxypropionate (3-HP), which is not normally detected at appreciable levels in healthy individuals (Matsumoto and Kuhara, 1996) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: 3-HP is an intermediate in the β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown pathway found in some vitamin B12-independent organisms.
source: Interestingly, 3-HP is an intermediate in the β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown pathway found in some vitamin B12-independent organisms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway diagram in Figure 1A and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia patients may break down propionate to some extent via an alternate oxidative route.
source: This observation suggests that propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia patients may break down propionate to some extent via an alternate oxidative route (Ando et al., 1972).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the observation of 3-HP in patients, supported by a citation.

claim: Numerous C. elegans metabolic genes are transcriptionally repressed in response to vitamin B12.
source: We previously identified numerous C. elegans metabolic genes that are transcriptionally repressed in response to vitamin B12 (MacNeil et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The C. elegans metabolic network is differentially wired under vitamin B12-deficient versus vitamin B12-replete nutritional conditions.
source: This finding suggests that the C. elegans metabolic network is differentially wired under vitamin B12-deficient versus vitamin B12-replete nutritional conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of differential gene expression in response to vitamin B12.

claim: C. elegans transcriptionally activates a β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown shunt under vitamin B12-deficient dietary conditions.
source: Here, we find that C. elegans transcriptionally activates a β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown shunt under vitamin B12-deficient dietary conditions, or under genetic conditions mimicking propionic- or methylmalonic acidemia.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and genetic experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C. elegans propionate shunt is chemically similar to, but genetically distinct from the pathway found in Candida albicans.
source: This pathway is chemically similar to, but genetically distinct from the pathway found in Candida albicans.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the pathways and the genes identified in C. elegans versus those known in C. albicans.

claim: Elevated 3-HP is detected in C. elegans animals with a dysfunctional canonical propionate breakdown pathway.
source: We detect elevated 3-HP in animals with a dysfunctional canonical propionate breakdown pathway, demonstrating that the C. elegans model faithfully recapitulates a metabolic phenotype of propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C. elegans model faithfully recapitulates a metabolic phenotype of propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia.
source: We detect elevated 3-HP in animals with a dysfunctional canonical propionate breakdown pathway, demonstrating that the C. elegans model faithfully recapitulates a metabolic phenotype of propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of elevated 3-HP in mutant animals, similar to what is seen in human patients.

claim: C. elegans is likely to encounter both vitamin B12-replete and B12-deficient diets in the wild because only a minority of bacterial species synthesize vitamin B12.
source: C. elegans is likely to encounter both vitamin B12-replete and B12-deficient diets in the wild because only a minority of bacterial species synthesize vitamin B12 (Karasseva et al., 1977; Sañudo-Wilhelmy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological considerations and supported by citations about bacterial vitamin B12 synthesis.

claim: Only a minority of bacterial species synthesize vitamin B12.
source: C. elegans is likely to encounter both vitamin B12-replete and B12-deficient diets in the wild because only a minority of bacterial species synthesize vitamin B12 (Karasseva et al., 1977; Sañudo-Wilhelmy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Activation of the C. elegans propionate shunt enables survival on vitamin B12-deficient diets.
source: We find that activation of the C. elegans propionate shunt enables survival on vitamin B12-deficient diets.
evidence: This is supported by survival and lethality assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Metabolic network rewiring in response to vitamin B12 status enables C. elegans to thrive both when dietary vitamin B12 is low and when this cofactor is in ample supply.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that metabolic network rewiring in response to vitamin B12 status enables the animal to thrive both when dietary vitamin B12 is low, and when this cofactor is in ample supply.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing differential pathway usage depending on B12 availability.

claim: Metabolic plasticity in propionate breakdown likely confers a selective advantage and evolutionary benefit to C. elegans.
source: This metabolic plasticity likely confers a selective advantage and evolutionary benefit.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: Patients with propionic acidemia harbor loss of function mutations in both alleles of either PCCA or PCCB.
source: Patients with propionic acidemia harbor loss of function mutations in both alleles of either PCCA or PCCB, which encode the two members of the propionyl-CoA carboxylase complex that catalyzes the first reaction in the canonical propionate breakdown pathway (Deodato et al., 2006) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PCCA and PCCB encode the two members of the propionyl-CoA carboxylase complex that catalyzes the first reaction in the canonical propionate breakdown pathway.
source: Patients with propionic acidemia harbor loss of function mutations in both alleles of either PCCA or PCCB, which encode the two members of the propionyl-CoA carboxylase complex that catalyzes the first reaction in the canonical propionate breakdown pathway (Deodato et al., 2006) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Propionic acidemia patients suffer from the toxic effects of propionate buildup, which manifest in several organ systems.
source: These patients suffer from the toxic effects of propionate buildup, which manifest in several organ systems and lead to acute symptoms such as poor feeding, vomiting, hypotonia, lethargy, seizures, failure to thrive, intellectual disability, pancreatitis and cardiomyopathy (Carrillo-Carrasco and Venditti, 2012).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Deletion of C. elegans pcca-1 slows development rate.
source: Deletion of the C. elegans ortholog of PCCA, pcca-1, slows development rate (Watson et al., 2014) and renders animal sensitive to propionate-induced toxicity: the LD50 of wild type animals is ~80mM propionate, while the LD50 of Δpcca-1 mutants is ~45 mM (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Deletion of C. elegans pcca-1 renders animals sensitive to propionate-induced toxicity.
source: Deletion of the C. elegans ortholog of PCCA, pcca-1, slows development rate (Watson et al., 2014) and renders animal sensitive to propionate-induced toxicity: the LD50 of wild type animals is ~80mM propionate, while the LD50 of Δpcca-1 mutants is ~45 mM (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The LD50 of wild type C. elegans for propionate is approximately 80mM.
source: Deletion of the C. elegans ortholog of PCCA, pcca-1, slows development rate (Watson et al., 2014) and renders animal sensitive to propionate-induced toxicity: the LD50 of wild type animals is ~80mM propionate, while the LD50 of Δpcca-1 mutants is ~45 mM (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The LD50 of Δpcca-1 mutants for propionate is approximately 45 mM.
source: Deletion of the C. elegans ortholog of PCCA, pcca-1, slows development rate (Watson et al., 2014) and renders animal sensitive to propionate-induced toxicity: the LD50 of wild type animals is ~80mM propionate, while the LD50 of Δpcca-1 mutants is ~45 mM (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation to wild type C. elegans increases propionate tolerance on the low-B12 E. coli OP50 diet.
source: As expected, vitamin B12 supplementation to wild type animals increases propionate tolerance on the low-B12 E. coli OP50 diet (Watson et al., 2014), whereas it has no beneficial effect in Δpcca-1 animals (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation has no beneficial effect on propionate tolerance in Δpcca-1 animals.
source: As expected, vitamin B12 supplementation to wild type animals increases propionate tolerance on the low-B12 E. coli OP50 diet (Watson et al., 2014), whereas it has no beneficial effect in Δpcca-1 animals (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The C. elegans acyl-CoA dehydrogenase acdh-1 transcript levels are very low when vitamin B12 is high.
source: The C. elegans acyl-CoA dehydrogenase acdh-1 is differentially expressed depending on the vitamin B12/propionate axis: its transcript levels are very low when vitamin B12 is high, and increase several hundred fold in response to propionate accumulation (Watson et al., 2013; 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: acdh-1 transcript levels increase several hundred fold in response to propionate accumulation.
source: The C. elegans acyl-CoA dehydrogenase acdh-1 is differentially expressed depending on the vitamin B12/propionate axis: its transcript levels are very low when vitamin B12 is high, and increase several hundred fold in response to propionate accumulation (Watson et al., 2013; 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: A null mutation in acdh-1 renders C. elegans sensitive to propionate with an LD50 of approximately 50 mM.
source: A null mutation in acdh-1 also renders C. elegans sensitive to propionate: the LD50 in these animals is ~50 mM (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Propionate sensitivity in Δacdh-1 mutants is completely rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation.
source: However, in contrast to Δpcca-1 mutants, propionate sensitivity in Δacdh-1 mutants is completely rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Δacdh-1 mutants exhibit embryonic lethality on a very low-vitamin B12 diet (E. coli OP50 grown on soy-peptone).
source: Furthermore, Δacdh-1 mutants exhibit embryonic lethality on a very low-vitamin B12 diet (E. coli OP50 grown on soy-peptone), and this phenotype can also be rescued by supplementing vitamin B12 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The embryonic lethality phenotype of Δacdh-1 mutants on very low-vitamin B12 diet can be rescued by supplementing vitamin B12.
source: Furthermore, Δacdh-1 mutants exhibit embryonic lethality on a very low-vitamin B12 diet (E. coli OP50 grown on soy-peptone), and this phenotype can also be rescued by supplementing vitamin B12 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenases catalyze the first step in β-oxidation of fatty acids.
source: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenases catalyze the first step in β-oxidation of fatty acids (Berg et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: acdh-1 may function in an alternate β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown pathway to enable survival of C. elegans on vitamin B12-deficient diets.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that acdh-1 may function in an alternate β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown pathway, hereafter referred to as the 'propionate shunt', to enable survival of the animal on vitamin B12-deficient diets.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed phenotypes and the known function of acyl-CoA dehydrogenases.

claim: Genes in parallel pathways often exhibit synthetic phenotypes.
source: Genes in parallel pathways often exhibit synthetic phenotypes (Clark et al., 1994; Costanzo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established genetic knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A cross between Δpcca-1 and Δacdh-1 mutants yielded no viable double homozygous mutant offspring.
source: However, a cross between Δpcca-1 and Δacdh-1 mutants yielded no viable double homozygous mutant offspring (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Loss of function in both pcca-1 and acdh-1 results in synthetic lethality.
source: This finding demonstrates that loss of function in both pcca-1 and acdh-1 results in synthetic lethality, and supports the hypothesis that acdh-1 functions in a parallel propionate breakdown pathway (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic cross data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RNAi of acdh-1 in the Δpcca-1 mutant resulted in complete lethality in the presence of 30 mM propionate.
source: RNAi of acdh-1 in the Δpcca-1 mutant resulted in complete lethality in the presence of 30 mM propionate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A synthetic genetic interaction screen identified three high-confidence hits: acdh-1, ech-6, and F09F7.4 (hach-1).
source: Only three high-confidence hits were obtained from this screen: acdh-1 itself, ech-6, an enoyl-CoA hydratase 6, and F09F7.4, which we named hach-1, for hydroxyacyl-CoA hydrolase (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the RNAi screen shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Enoyl-CoA hydratases function in the second step of β-oxidation.
source: Enoyl-CoA hydratases function in the second step of β-oxidation (Berg et al., 2012) and, therefore, ech-6 is an excellent candidate to catalyze the second reaction in the propionate shunt, directly downstream of acdh-1.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: ech-6 is a candidate to catalyze the second reaction in the propionate shunt, directly downstream of acdh-1.
source: Enoyl-CoA hydratases function in the second step of β-oxidation (Berg et al., 2012) and, therefore, ech-6 is an excellent candidate to catalyze the second reaction in the propionate shunt, directly downstream of acdh-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of enoyl-CoA hydratases and the genetic screen results.

claim: In C. albicans, the Ehd3 enzyme converts 3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA into 3-HP and CoA in the third step of the β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown pathway.
source: In the vitamin B12-independent yeast C. albicans, the Ehd3 enzyme converts 3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA into 3-HP and CoA in the third step of the β-oxidation-like propionate breakdown pathway (Otzen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the C. albicans pathway supported by a citation.

claim: Ehd3 is the one-to-one ortholog of hach-1.
source: Ehd3 is the one-to-one ortholog of hach-1, the third gene we identified, which we therefore placed downstream of ech-6.
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis.

claim: Knockdown of either ech-6 or hach-1 resulted in increased propionate sensitivity that was partially rescued by the addition of vitamin B12.
source: Importantly, knockdown of either ech-6 or hach-1 resulted in similar phenotypes compared to loss of acdh-1: increased propionate sensitivity that was partially rescued by the addition of vitamin B12 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The first reaction of the propionate shunt produces acrylyl-CoA, a highly toxic and reactive metabolite.
source: The first reaction of the propionate shunt produces acrylyl-CoA, a highly toxic and reactive metabolite (Hellwig et al., 1993; Saillenfait et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about acrylyl-CoA toxicity supported by citations.

claim: RNAi of ech-6 strongly reduces C. elegans growth and viability.
source: Indeed, RNAi of ech-6, and to a lesser extent hach-1, strongly reduces C. elegans growth and viability (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The severe phenotype of ech-6 RNAi was partially rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation.
source: This phenotype was partially rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation, which facilitates propionate flux through the canonical pathway (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Vitamin B12 supplementation had no beneficial effect when ech-6 or hach-1 was knocked down in Δpcca-1 mutants.
source: This rescue depends on a functional canonical B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway, as vitamin B12 supplementation had no beneficial effect when ech-6 or hach-1 was knocked down in Δpcca-1 mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Loss of acdh-1 largely suppressed the phenotypic effects of ech-6 and hach-1 knockdown.
source: We found that loss of acdh-1 largely suppressed the phenotypic effects of ech-6 and hach-1 knockdown, likely due to the lack of acrylyl-CoA production in the absence of acdh-1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The genetic buffering of ech-6 and hach-1 knockdown by loss of acdh-1 supports the placement of ech-6 and hach-1 downstream of acdh-1 in the propionate shunt.
source: This genetic buffering supports the placement of ech-6 and hach-1 downstream of acdh-1 in the propionate shunt (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic buffering data.

claim: The gene encoding the enzyme that converts 3-HP into MSA has not yet been identified in any metazoan.
source: Importantly, the gene encoding the enzyme that converts 3-HP into MSA has not yet been identified in any metazoan.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: WISP predicted Y38F1A.6 and alh-8 as top functional connections to acdh-1, ech-6 and hach-1.
source: To identify enzymes that may catalyze the last two reactions in the C. elegans propionate shunt, we utilized WISP, a server for predicting tissue-specific functional networks based on the integration of a large compendium of diverse datasets (http://wisp.princeton.edu, Yao et al., in preparation; V. Yao, personal communication, June 2016). The top predicted functional connections to acdh-1, ech-6 and hach-1 included the metabolic genes Y38F1A.6 and alh-8 (Figure 4A), neither of which was tested in genetic interaction screen because they were not included in the ORFeome RNAi library (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on computational network analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Y38F1A.6 is the ortholog of human ADHFE1 (also known as HOT), a hydroxyacid-oxoacid transhydrogenase.
source: Y38F1A.6 is the ortholog of human ADHFE1 (also known as HOT), a hydroxyacid-oxoacid transhydrogenase that has been found to metabolize β-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a structural analog of 3-HP (Lyon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis and supported by a citation about ADHFE1 function.

claim: ADHFE1 has been found to metabolize β-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a structural analog of 3-HP.
source: Y38F1A.6 is the ortholog of human ADHFE1 (also known as HOT), a hydroxyacid-oxoacid transhydrogenase that has been found to metabolize β-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a structural analog of 3-HP (Lyon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADHFE1 function supported by a citation.

claim: ALH-8 is homologous to human ALDH6A1, a decarboxylating dehydrogenase.
source: ALH-8 is homologous to human ALDH6A1, a decarboxylating dehydrogenase predicted to act on two structurally similar metabolites: methylmalonic semialdehyde from valine breakdown (Marcadier et al., 2013; Sass et al., 2012), and malonic semialdehyde (Marcadier et al., 2013), the substrate in the fifth reaction of the propionate oxidation pathway (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on homology analysis and supported by citations about ALDH6A1 function.

claim: ALDH6A1 is predicted to act on methylmalonic semialdehyde from valine breakdown and malonic semialdehyde.
source: ALH-8 is homologous to human ALDH6A1, a decarboxylating dehydrogenase predicted to act on two structurally similar metabolites: methylmalonic semialdehyde from valine breakdown (Marcadier et al., 2013; Sass et al., 2012), and malonic semialdehyde (Marcadier et al., 2013), the substrate in the fifth reaction of the propionate oxidation pathway (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ALDH6A1 function supported by citations.

claim: hphd-1, acdh-1, ech-6, and hach-1 are predicted to localize to the mitochondria.
source: Additionally, hphd-1 and alh-8 are predicted to localize to the mitochondria along with acdh-1, ech-6, and hach-1 (Yilmaz and Walhout, 2016; http://wormflux.umassmed.edu/).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions cited from a database.

claim: alh-8 is predicted to localize to the mitochondria.
source: Additionally, hphd-1 and alh-8 are predicted to localize to the mitochondria along with acdh-1, ech-6, and hach-1 (Yilmaz and Walhout, 2016; http://wormflux.umassmed.edu/).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions cited from a database.

claim: An alh-8 deletion mutant was generated by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing.
source: We obtained an hphd-1 deletion mutant from the C. elegans genetics center, and generated an alh-8 deletion mutant by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing (Kim et al., 2014) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both Δhphd-1 and Δalh-8 mutants exhibited decreased propionate tolerance that was at least partially rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation.
source: Both mutants phenocopied acdh-1, ech-6 and hach-1 loss of functions: they exhibited decreased propionate tolerance that was at least partially rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both Δhphd-1 and Δalh-8 mutants displayed partial lethality on low-B12 diets.
source: Both Δhphd-1 and Δalh-8 mutants displayed partial lethality on low-B12 diets, which was rescued by vitamin B12 supplementation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Vitamin B12 failed to rescue the partial larval lethality exhibited by the double Δhphd-1;Δpcca-1 mutant.
source: This rescue was dependent on a functional canonical propionate breakdown pathway, as vitamin B12 failed to rescue the partial larval lethality exhibited by the double Δhphd-1;Δpcca-1 mutant (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Activation of the propionate shunt is required to sustain viability in C. elegans.
source: This result indicates that activation of the propionate shunt is required to sustain viability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that vitamin B12 cannot rescue the double mutant.

claim: Δhphd-1;Δpcca-1 mutants exhibited increased propionate sensitivity compared to either single mutant.
source: Δhphd-1;Δpcca-1 mutants also exhibited increased propionate sensitivity compared to either single mutant, indicating a conditional genetic interaction between hphd-1 and pcca-1, but not complete lethality like the Δacdh-1;Δpcca-1 double mutant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Δhphd-1 may not be a complete null allele.
source: This may be due to Δhphd-1 not being completely null, or it is possible that an intact half-pathway is sufficient for at least partial survival.
evidence: This is speculation about why the double mutant phenotype is not as severe as expected.

claim: Reduced expression of all five shunt genes by vitamin B12 is reversed by supplementation of excess propionate.
source: Indeed, we found that reduced expression of all five shunt genes by vitamin B12 is reversed by supplementation of excess propionate (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Activation of acdh-1 in response to propionate buildup occurs through its 1.5 kb promoter, indicating transcriptional regulation.
source: Activation of acdh-1 in response to propionate buildup occurs through its 1.5 kb promoter, indicating that it is governed by transcriptional mechanisms (Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work using a promoter-GFP reporter.

claim: The acdh-1 promoter is activated by propionate and by canonical pathway perturbations.
source: Not only is the acdh-1 promoter activated by propionate and by canonical pathway perturbations, it is also activated by perturbation of the propionate shunt genes ech-6, hach-1 and acdh-1 itself (Watson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of hphd-1 led to greater acdh-1 promoter activity.
source: Loss of hphd-1 did in fact lead to greater acdh-1 promoter activity, providing additional evidence that hphd-1 functions in propionate breakdown (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: 3-HP is a unique metabolic intermediate produced by the propionate oxidation pathway in metazoans.
source: 3-HP is a unique metabolic intermediate produced by the propionate oxidation pathway: to our knowledge neither KEGG, nor any other metabolic database, lists this metabolite being produced by any other metabolic pathway in metazoans, though it can be produced through several different pathways in microorganisms.
evidence: This is based on analysis of metabolic databases.

claim: The fourth reaction in the propionate shunt involves the conversion of 3-HP into MSA.
source: The fourth reaction in the propionate shunt involves the conversion of 3-HP into MSA (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in the pathway diagram in Figure 6A.

claim: 3-HP was detected in C. elegans but not in its E. coli diet.
source: Using liquid chromatography/selective reaction monitoring mass spectrometry (LC-SRM) we detected 3-HP in C. elegans, but not in its E. coli diet (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ample propionyl-CoA was detected in E. coli supplemented with propionate.
source: We did detect ample propionyl-CoA in E. coli supplemented with propionate, so the lack of 3-HP in E. coli was not due to lack of pathway substrate (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 3-HP detected is derived from C. elegans and not from its bacterial diet.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the 3-HP detected is derived from C. elegans and not from its bacterial diet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that 3-HP is present in worms but not in bacteria.

claim: A >4-fold increase in 3-HP levels was observed in Δpcca-1 mutants.
source: We observed a >4-fold increase in 3-HP levels in Δpcca-1 mutants, which mirrors elevated 3-HP levels observed in human patients with propionic acidemia caused by PCCA or PCCB mutations (Carrillo-Carrasco and Venditti, 2012), and confirms that the propionate shunt is active when the canonical pathway is perturbed (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Elevated 3-HP levels in Δpcca-1 mutants mirrors elevated 3-HP levels observed in human patients with propionic acidemia.
source: We observed a >4-fold increase in 3-HP levels in Δpcca-1 mutants, which mirrors elevated 3-HP levels observed in human patients with propionic acidemia caused by PCCA or PCCB mutations (Carrillo-Carrasco and Venditti, 2012), and confirms that the propionate shunt is active when the canonical pathway is perturbed (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with human patient data, supported by a citation.

claim: A >200-fold increase in 3-HP levels was detected in Δhphd-1 mutants.
source: Importantly, we detected a >200-fold increase in 3-HP levels in Δhphd-1 mutants, which supports our prediction that HPHD-1 metabolizes 3-HP under low B12 conditions (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: The >200-fold increase in 3-HP in Δhphd-1 mutants supports the prediction that HPHD-1 metabolizes 3-HP.
source: Importantly, we detected a >200-fold increase in 3-HP levels in Δhphd-1 mutants, which supports our prediction that HPHD-1 metabolizes 3-HP under low B12 conditions (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the accumulation of 3-HP when hphd-1 is deleted.

claim: 13C-3-HP was detected after feeding Δhphd-1 mutant animals E. coli OP50 supplemented with 13C-propionate for 2 hr.
source: To verify that 3-HP is indeed derived from propionate, we performed carbon tracing by feeding Δhphd-1 mutant animals E. coli OP50 supplemented with 13C-propionate. We detected the formation of 13C-3-HP after 2 hr, demonstrating that C. elegans indeed converts propionate to 3-HP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by carbon tracing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: C. elegans converts propionate to 3-HP.
source: To verify that 3-HP is indeed derived from propionate, we performed carbon tracing by feeding Δhphd-1 mutant animals E. coli OP50 supplemented with 13C-propionate. We detected the formation of 13C-3-HP after 2 hr, demonstrating that C. elegans indeed converts propionate to 3-HP (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the carbon tracing experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 3-HP is a specific diagnostic marker of propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias.
source: 3-HP is a specific diagnostic marker of propionic- and methylmalonic acidemias, as it is uniquely elevated in these diseases.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: An alternative propionate breakdown pathway may be operational in humans, at least in patients with impaired canonical propionate breakdown.
source: This suggests that an alternative propionate breakdown pathway may be operational in humans as well, at least in patients with impaired canonical propionate breakdown.
evidence: This is speculation based on the detection of 3-HP in human patients.

claim: The closest human homologs of several C. elegans shunt enzymes are known to catalyze structurally similar reactions in other metabolic pathways, including the breakdown of branched chain amino acids.
source: Interestingly, the closest human homologs of the C. elegans shunt enzymes are known to catalyze structurally similar reactions in other metabolic pathways, including the breakdown of the branched chain amino acids isoleucine and valine (Figure 7A-Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on comparison of enzyme functions shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Patients with mutations in ALDH6A1 exhibit elevated levels of 3-HP as well as elevated levels of valine breakdown intermediates.
source: Further, patients with mutations in ALDH6A1 (the homolog of C. elegans alh-8) exhibit elevated levels of 3-HP as well as elevated levels of valine breakdown intermediates (Marcadier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from patient metabolomics studies supported by a citation.

claim: The closest human homologs of several C. elegans propionate shunt genes may have conserved roles in propionate breakdown in humans in addition to their known roles in other pathways.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the closest human homologs of several C. elegans propionate shunt genes may have conserved roles in propionate breakdown in humans in addition to their known roles in other pathways.
evidence: This is speculation based on the metabolomics data from human patients.

claim: The closest human homologs of all five propionate shunt genes (ACADSB, ECHS1, HIBCH, ADHFE1 and ALDH6A1) are significantly co-expressed in both mouse and human.
source: We found that the closest human homologs of all five propionate shunt genes, ACADSB, ECHS1, HIBCH, ADHFE1 and ALDH6A1 are significantly co-expressed in both mouse and human across a large compendium of transcriptomic data in the SEEK database (Figure 7B) (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by co-expression analysis shown in Figure 7B and a citation to the SEEK database.

claim: The human homologs of C. elegans propionate shunt genes may be co-regulated at the transcriptional level.
source: This suggests that, like their C. elegans counterparts, these human genes may be co-regulated at the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed co-expression.

claim: The expression of ADHFE1, HIBCH, and to a lesser extent ECHS1 and ALDH6A1, is upregulated in response to propionate in HepG2 cells.
source: Remarkably, the expression of ADHFE1, HIBCH, and to a lesser extent ECHS1 and ALDH6A1, is upregulated in response to propionate in HepG2 cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The regulated response of human propionate shunt gene homologs to propionate at the gene expression level is at least to some extent conserved between C. elegans and humans.
source: These data suggest that the regulated response of these genes to propionate at the gene expression level is, at least to some extent, conserved between C. elegans and humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of propionate-induced expression in both organisms.

claim: This study presents the first example of transcriptional metabolic network rewiring in which the catabolic route of a cellular metabolite is dictated by the presence or absence of a dietary vitamin.
source: To our knowledge, our study presents the first example of transcriptional metabolic network rewiring in which the catabolic route of a cellular metabolite is dictated by the presence or absence of a dietary vitamin, in this case vitamin B12.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Vitamins A and D have known roles in regulating gene expression that are important for development, growth and homeostasis.
source: Other vitamins that have known roles in regulating gene expression include vitamins A and D, and this regulation is important for development, growth and homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vitamin function.

claim: Vitamins A and D do not function directly in the metabolic network as cofactors of metabolic enzymes, and instead function more like hormones.
source: However, vitamins A and D do not function directly in the metabolic network as cofactors of metabolic enzymes, and instead function more like hormones; in fact vitamin D can be synthesized endogenously.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vitamin function.

claim: Vitamin D, via the vitamin D receptor (VDR), regulates mineral uptake.
source: Vitamin D, via the vitamin D receptor (VDR), regulates mineral uptake (Carlberg and Seuter, 2009; Haussler et al., 2008), while vitamin A, via the retinoic acid receptor (RAR), regulates developmental programs as well as the enzymes that interconvert the regulatory version of retinoic acid and the trans-retinal version required by rhodopsin for light-sensing (D'Aniello and Waxman, 2015; di Masi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Vitamin A, via the retinoic acid receptor (RAR), regulates developmental programs as well as the enzymes that interconvert the regulatory version of retinoic acid and the trans-retinal version required by rhodopsin for light-sensing.
source: Vitamin D, via the vitamin D receptor (VDR), regulates mineral uptake (Carlberg and Seuter, 2009; Haussler et al., 2008), while vitamin A, via the retinoic acid receptor (RAR), regulates developmental programs as well as the enzymes that interconvert the regulatory version of retinoic acid and the trans-retinal version required by rhodopsin for light-sensing (D'Aniello and Waxman, 2015; di Masi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Gene expression profiling in mammalian cells has revealed transcript-level responses to vitamins B1, B2, B3, B6, B9, C, and E.
source: However, gene expression profiling in mammalian cells has revealed transcript-level responses to vitamins B1 (thiamine) (Fraser et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2004) (Tanaka et al., 2007), B2 (riboflavin) (Nakano et al., 2011), B3 (nicotinamide/niacin) (Choi et al., 2011; Couturier et al., 2014; Giammona et al., 2006), B6 (pyridoxal 5′ phosphate, PLP) (Toya et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014), B9 (folic acid) (Barua et al., 2014; Champier et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2011), C (ascorbic acid) (Canali et al., 2014; Jun et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2014), and E (tocopherol/tocotrienols) (Landrier et al., 2010; Makpol et al., 2013; Mustacich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mechanisms behind, and consequences of, vitamin-induced gene expression changes have yet to be elucidated for most vitamins.
source: The mechanisms behind, and consequences of, these observed vitamin-induced gene expression changes have yet to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In C. elegans, low vitamin B12 leads to accumulation of propionate due to reduced flux through the B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway.
source: Our study indicates that, in C. elegans, low vitamin B12 leads to accumulation of the short chain fatty acid propionate due to reduced flux through the B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: It remains to be determined whether vitamin B12 is directly sensed or whether propionate or one of its derivatives is the sole proxy regulator.
source: It remains to be determined whether vitamin B12 is directly sensed similar to vitamins A and D, or whether propionate or perhaps one of its derivatives is the sole proxy regulator (see below).
evidence: This is a statement about what is not yet known.

claim: In mammals, propionate and other short chain fatty acids produced by the gut microbiota provide numerous benefits to the host.
source: In mammals, propionate and other short chain fatty acids produced by the gut microbiota provide numerous benefits to the host, not only as nutrient sources that fuel colonocytes, but also potentially to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce cancer cell apoptosis (Emenaker et al., 2001; Hinnebusch et al., 2002), and reduce inflammation (Louis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Excess propionate accumulation, which occurs in patients with propionic- or methylmalonic acidemia, is toxic.
source: However, excess propionate accumulation, which occurs in patients with propionic- or methylmalonic acidemia, is toxic.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: The metabolic network rewiring in C. elegans in response to the vitamin B12/propionate axis may have evolved to optimize energy yield from propionate depending on B12 availability and to prevent toxic propionate buildup.
source: It is possible that the metabolic network rewiring that we observe in C. elegans in response to the vitamin B12/propionate axis has evolved not only to optimize energy yield from propionate depending on the presence or absence of B12, but also to prevent toxic propionate buildup.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: This represents a novel example of built-in metabolic network flexibility to mitigate the toxic accumulation of an endogenous metabolite.
source: This represents a novel example of built-in metabolic network flexibility to mitigate the toxic accumulation of an endogenous metabolite.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: A loss of propionate breakdown capability in double Δpcca-1/Δacdh-1 mutants is not compatible with viability.
source: A loss of propionate breakdown capability, in double Δpcca-1/Δacdh-1 mutants, or in Δacdh-1 mutants on a very low vitamin B12 diet (E. coli OP50 grown on soy peptone) is not compatible with viability (this study).
evidence: This is supported by the genetic and survival data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vitamin B12 is exclusively produced by bacteria.
source: Vitamin B12 is exclusively produced by bacteria, and studies of microbial communities have found that only 20–30% of community members synthesize vitamin B12 (Sañudo-Wilhelmy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Studies of microbial communities have found that only 20–30% of community members synthesize vitamin B12.
source: Vitamin B12 is exclusively produced by bacteria, and studies of microbial communities have found that only 20–30% of community members synthesize vitamin B12 (Sañudo-Wilhelmy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: C. elegans is found all over the world in temperate climates and is likely to feed on a variety of bacterial species.
source: C. elegans is found all over the world in temperate climates and is likely to feed on a variety of bacterial species (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans ecology supported by a citation.

claim: The ability to catabolize propionate whether or not vitamin B12 is provided by the diet may provide C. elegans with the metabolic flexibility to survive in different dietary conditions, thus providing a selective advantage and evolutionary benefit.
source: Our data suggest that the ability to catabolize propionate whether or not vitamin B12 is provided by the diet may provide the animal with the metabolic flexibility to survive in different dietary conditions, thus providing a selective advantage and evolutionary benefit.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary significance based on the experimental findings.

claim: On vitamin B12-replete bacterial diets, such as Comamonas aquatica, expression of the propionate shunt is greatly reduced.
source: On vitamin B12-replete bacterial diets, such as Comamonas aquatica, expression of the propionate shunt is greatly reduced, indicating that the canonical vitamin B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway is preferred.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The canonical vitamin B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway is preferred over the propionate shunt on B12-replete diets.
source: On vitamin B12-replete bacterial diets, such as Comamonas aquatica, expression of the propionate shunt is greatly reduced, indicating that the canonical vitamin B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway is preferred.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene expression patterns.

claim: The canonical pathway may be more efficient at metabolizing propionyl-CoA than the propionate shunt due to the high redox potential between propionyl-CoA and acrylyl-CoA.
source: We speculate that this may be because the canonical pathway is more efficient at metabolizing propionyl-CoA than the propionate shunt due to the high redox potential between propionyl-CoA and acrylyl-CoA, the first shunt pathway intermediate (Sato et al., 1999).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation about redox potential.

claim: Advantages of the canonical pathway over the shunt include the use of fewer enzymes and the lack of production of highly toxic intermediates.
source: Other advantages of the canonical pathway over the shunt include the use of fewer enzymes, and the lack of production of highly toxic intermediates (e.g., acrylyl-CoA).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the two pathways.

claim: The severity of phenotypes from propionate shunt gene disruptions differs depending on the gene disruption.
source: While all of the five genes identified in this study as propionate shunt members lead to similar phenotypes when mutated or knocked down (sensitivity to propionate-induced toxicity and at least partial lethality on B12-deficient diets), the severity of these phenotypes differs depending on the gene disruption.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data.

claim: Different levels of reactivity and toxicity among the intermediates in the pathway may explain the different severity of phenotypes.
source: This could potentially be explained by different levels of reactivity (and therefore toxicity) among the intermediates in the pathway, which may accumulate to different levels depending on which enzyme is disrupted.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed phenotypic differences.

claim: ech-6 knockdown results in a very severe phenotype, likely due to the accumulation of its substrate acrylyl-CoA, which is highly toxic.
source: For instance, ech-6 knockdown results in a very severe phenotype, likely due to the accumulation of its substrate acrylyl-CoA, which is highly toxic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotype and the known toxicity of acrylyl-CoA.

claim: The buildup of substrates containing CoA could lead to widespread metabolic impairment due to CoA sequestration.
source: Simultaneously, the buildup of substrates containing CoA could lead to widespread metabolic impairment due to CoA sequestration (Mitchell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation about CoA sequestration.

claim: Several enzymes that function in the shunt may also have roles in isoleucine and valine breakdown, and may therefore be pleiotropic.
source: Additionally, several enzymes that function in the shunt may also have roles in isoleucine and valine breakdown, and may therefore be pleiotropic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of the human homologs.

claim: The Δhphd-1 and Δalh-8 deletion mutants may not be null since they are both partial locus deletions.
source: It should be mentioned that the Δhphd-1 and Δalh-8 deletion mutants used in this study may not be null since they are both partial locus deletions, and this may explain the less severe phenotypes observed for these mutants compared with the null Δacdh-1 mutant.
evidence: This is speculation about the nature of the mutant alleles.

claim: C. elegans can somewhat tolerate B12 deficiency with only a partially intact shunt consisting of the first three reactions.
source: It is also possible that C. elegans can (somewhat) tolerate B12 deficiency with only a partially intact shunt consisting of the first three reactions, or that there are other unidentified (partially) redundant enzymes that can compensate for loss of hphd-1 and alh-8.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for the observed phenotypes.

claim: Each of the five genes that encode enzymes of the propionate shunt is repressed by vitamin B12 and activated by propionate.
source: Each of the five genes that encode enzymes of the propionate shunt is repressed by vitamin B12 and activated by propionate.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The response of acdh-1 occurs at the level of transcriptional regulation.
source: By using a GFP reporter driven by 1.5 kb of acdh-1 promoter DNA we previously found that GFP levels are high when animals are fed bacterial diets low in vitamin B12, whereas GFP is greatly reduced when the animals are fed bacteria that synthesize high levels of vitamin B12, or upon direct supplementation of vitamin B12 (MacNeil et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2013; Watson et al., 2014). This demonstrated that the response of acdh-1 occurs at the level of transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work using a promoter-GFP reporter.

claim: Vitamin B12 is not sufficient to repress the acdh-1 promoter when enzymes within the B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway are genetically perturbed.
source: Vitamin B12 is not sufficient to repress the acdh-1 promoter when enzymes within the B12-dependent propionate breakdown pathway are genetically perturbed, or when excess propionate is added to the media (Watson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The C. elegans gene regulatory network activates acdh-1 expression in response to the buildup of propionate, which occurs when vitamin B12 is in low supply.
source: Therefore, we propose that the C. elegans gene regulatory network activates acdh-1 expression in response to the buildup of propionate, which occurs when this vitamin is in low supply.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed gene expression patterns.

claim: More than 50 C. elegans transcription factors regulate acdh-1.
source: We have previously identified more than 50 C. elegans transcription factors that regulate acdh-1 (MacNeil et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2013), including the nuclear hormone receptor NHR-10 that directly binds its promoter (Arda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The nuclear hormone receptor NHR-10 directly binds the acdh-1 promoter.
source: We have previously identified more than 50 C. elegans transcription factors that regulate acdh-1 (MacNeil et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2013), including the nuclear hormone receptor NHR-10 that directly binds its promoter (Arda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nuclear hormone receptors utilize binding to small molecule ligands to regulate gene expression.
source: Nuclear hormone receptors utilize binding to small molecule ligands to regulate gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear hormone receptor function.

claim: VDR directly interacts with vitamin D, and RAR binds biologically active forms of vitamin A.
source: For instance, VDR directly interacts with vitamin D, and RAR binds biologically active forms of vitamin A (Carlberg, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Humans have 48 nuclear hormone receptors.
source: While humans have 48 nuclear hormone receptors, C. elegans has more than 270 (Reece-Hoyes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: C. elegans has more than 270 nuclear hormone receptors.
source: While humans have 48 nuclear hormone receptors, C. elegans has more than 270 (Reece-Hoyes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: One or more C. elegans nuclear hormone receptors may directly respond to propionate or propionyl-CoA.
source: It is tempting to speculate that one or more C. elegans nuclear hormone receptors directly respond to propionate, or its CoA derivative propionyl-CoA.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of transcriptional regulation.

claim: Several lines of evidence indicate that humans also utilize a propionate detox shunt, at least to some extent.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that humans also utilize a propionate detox shunt, at least to some extent.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The detection of 3-HP is used as a diagnostic marker for propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia in newborns.
source: First, the detection of the unique shunt intermediate 3-HP is used as a diagnostic marker for propionic- and methylmalonic acidemia in newborns.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: 3-HP is not predicted as an intermediate in any other metazoan pathway.
source: Since 3-HP is not predicted as an intermediate in any other metazoan pathway, this finding suggests that a propionate shunt may also be functional in humans.
evidence: This is based on analysis of metabolic databases.

claim: Global metabolomics has identified 3-HP in healthy individuals.
source: Interestingly, global metabolomics has identified 3-HP in healthy individuals (Bouatra et al., 2013; Guneral and Bachmann, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The propionate shunt may be part of central metabolism in humans.
source: This finding suggests that the propionate shunt may also be active to some degree when the canonical pathway is functional and thus may be part of central metabolism in humans.
evidence: This is speculation based on the detection of 3-HP in healthy individuals.

claim: Patients with an impaired canonical propionate breakdown pathway are very sick and must strictly adhere to diets low in the amino acids that are broken down to propionyl-CoA.
source: It is important to note that, in spite of evidence supporting alternative propionate breakdown mechanisms in humans, patients with an impaired canonical propionate breakdown pathway are very sick and must strictly adhere to diets low in the amino acids that are broken down to propionyl-CoA.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: In humans, alternative propionate catabolism routes are not sufficient to maintain propionate levels below the toxic threshold.
source: This indicates that, in humans, alternative propionate catabolism routes are not sufficient to maintain propionate levels below the toxic threshold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical severity of propionic and methylmalonic acidemias.

claim: hphd-1 is the first metazoan gene to be associated with the reaction catalyzed by 3-hydroypropionate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.59).
source: hphd-1 is the first metazoan gene to be associated with the reaction catalyzed by 3-hydroypropionate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.59), which converts 3-HP to MSA.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: ADHFE1 is thought to metabolize GHB, which is commonly known as a recreational drug.
source: ADHFE1 is thought to metabolize a structural analog of 3-HP, GHB, which is commonly known as a recreational drug.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADHFE1 function.

claim: ADHFE1 is not assigned by KEGG or BRENDA enzyme databases to any endogenous metabolic pathway.
source: However ADHFE1 is not assigned by KEGG or BRENDA enzyme databases to any endogenous metabolic pathway.
evidence: This is based on analysis of enzyme databases.

claim: ADHFE1 transfers electrons to the TCA cycle intermediate α-ketoglutarate, thereby producing (D)-2-hydroxyglutarate.
source: ADHFE1 is unique in that, unlike most dehydrogenases that transfer electrons from their substrates to NAD or FAD, it transfers electrons to the TCA cycle intermediate α-ketoglutarate, thereby producing (D)-2-hydroxyglutarate (Struys et al., 2005), a putative oncometabolite (Dang et al., 2009; Kranendijk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ADHFE1 function supported by citations.

claim: (D)-2-hydroxyglutarate is a putative oncometabolite.
source: ADHFE1 is unique in that, unlike most dehydrogenases that transfer electrons from their substrates to NAD or FAD, it transfers electrons to the TCA cycle intermediate α-ketoglutarate, thereby producing (D)-2-hydroxyglutarate (Struys et al., 2005), a putative oncometabolite (Dang et al., 2009; Kranendijk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Other than neomorphic IDH enzyme mutants found in many cancers, ADHFE1 is the only known enzyme to naturally produce (D)-2-hydroxyglutarate.
source: Interestingly, other than neomorphic isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) enzyme mutants found in many cancers, ADHFE1 is the only known enzyme to naturally produce (D)-2-hydroxyglutarate (Struys et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: No patients have been identified with mutations in ADHFE1.
source: Currently, no patients have been identified with mutations in ADHFE1 so there is no metabolomics data available to determine which metabolites build up in humans lacking ADHFE1 enzyme function.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of clinical knowledge.

claim: hphd-1 and ADHFE1 are clear one-to-one orthologs.
source: However, our C. elegans mass spectrometry data in mutants lacking hphd-1 revealed greatly elevated 3-HP levels (Figure 5), and, since hphd-1 and ADHFE1 are clear one-to-one orthologs, ADHFE1 is a good candidate to function in propionate oxidation in humans directly downstream of 3-HP.
evidence: This is based on orthology analysis.

claim: ADHFE1 is a good candidate to function in propionate oxidation in humans directly downstream of 3-HP.
source: However, our C. elegans mass spectrometry data in mutants lacking hphd-1 revealed greatly elevated 3-HP levels (Figure 5), and, since hphd-1 and ADHFE1 are clear one-to-one orthologs, ADHFE1 is a good candidate to function in propionate oxidation in humans directly downstream of 3-HP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the C. elegans data and orthology.
